cards.question: How does Kotlin null safety work at compile time?
cards.answer: Regular types exclude null; nullable types append ? and require safe calls or checks before use. The compiler rejects many NPE-prone patterns Java allows. !! asserts non-null and throws if wrong. Prefer Elvis defaults and let for smart casts after guards.

cards.question: What is the difference between val and var?
cards.answer: val declares read-only references; reassignment is forbidden though mutable objects may still mutate internally. var allows rebinding to another instance. Use val by default for clearer intent and safer concurrency. Immutable data structures pair well with val fields in data classes.

cards.question: When use data class versus regular class?
cards.answer: data class auto-generates equals, hashCode, toString, copy, and componentN for properties in the primary constructor. Ideal for DTOs and value objects without heavy invariants. Regular classes suit entities with behavior and encapsulation. data class copy helps immutable updates in Redux-style state.

cards.question: Explain sealed classes and sealed interfaces.
cards.answer: Subtypes are known at compile time within the same module, enabling exhaustive when without else. Model UI states, network results, and domain events cleanly. Unlike enum, subclasses can carry distinct property sets. sealed interface supports multiple inheritance of contracts in Kotlin 1.5+.

cards.question: What are extension functions and their limitations?
cards.answer: They add methods to existing types without inheritance, resolved statically at compile time. Cannot access private members of the extended class. Useful for DSL builders and adapting third-party APIs. Overuse scatters API surface; prefer cohesive types for domain logic.

cards.question: How do scope functions let, run, with, apply, also differ?
cards.answer: They execute blocks with a receiver or argument and return different values for chaining ergonomics. apply returns the receiver after configuration; also returns receiver after side effects for logging. let passes it as argument and returns block result, great for nullables. Choose based on readability, not brevity alone.

cards.question: What is inline reified generics and where is it used?
cards.answer: inline functions with reified T preserve type at runtime without JVM erasure in that scope. Enables type checks and Gson/Moshi style adapters without passing Class objects manually. Only works with inline functions, not regular generics. Common in Android startActivity and Ktor routing helpers.

cards.question: Compare lazy delegation versus lateinit.
cards.answer: lazy initializes on first access thread-safely by default for val properties. lateinit var marks non-null reference initialized later before use, mainly for injected fields on Android. lateinit fails fast on access if unset; lazy throws on circular initialization. lateinit cannot hold primitives.

cards.question: What are value classes and why use them?
cards.answer: Inline value classes wrap a single property with zero overhead when used as that property at runtime on JVM. Model type-safe IDs like UserId versus raw Long. Prevents argument swaps in large function lists. JVM name mangling applies when boxed or used as generics.

cards.question: How does Kotlin handle equality with ==?
cards.answer: == calls structural equals unless comparing nullable Any where reference equality may apply for some cases; === is referential identity. Data classes implement equals on properties. Floating point compares follow IEEE unless you normalize. Collections use element-wise equals for listOf comparisons.

Define ownership boundaries, observability, and rollback paths before scaling usage across services or devices. Expect follow-ups on failure isolation, security, and long-term cost once null safety becomes load-bearing.

categories.name: Coroutines & Flow
categories.description: Structured concurrency, dispatchers, flows, and cancellation on JVM and mobile.

cards.question: What is a coroutine versus a thread on the JVM?
cards.answer: Coroutines are lightweight tasks scheduled by kotlinx.coroutines on thread pools. Thousands can run without one OS thread each. Suspend functions pause without blocking threads during IO waits. Threads remain the underlying workers; coroutines add structured async style.

cards.question: Explain structured concurrency with coroutineScope and supervisorScope.
cards.answer: Child jobs fail the parent scope by default, cancelling siblings in coroutineScope. supervisorScope isolates child failures so one error does not cancel peers. launch and async inherit parent context and cancellation. Always tie work to a scope lifecycle like viewModelScope or request scope.

cards.question: When choose Dispatchers.IO versus Default versus Main?
cards.answer: IO is for blocking or high-latency IO with an expanded pool. Default runs CPU-bound work sized to cores. Main posts to UI thread on Android or JavaFX. withContext switches dispatcher for a block without leaking wrong thread assumptions.

cards.question: How does cancellation propagate in coroutines?
cards.answer: Cancelling a Job cancels children and throws CancellationException at suspension points. Cooperative cancellation requires checking isActive or using cancellable suspending APIs. Non-cancellable finally runs with withContext(NonCancellable) for cleanup. Blocking Java calls ignore cancellation unless wrapped with interruptible patterns.

cards.question: What is Flow and how differs from RxJava cold streams?
cards.answer: Flow is cold: collectors trigger execution; multiple collectors re-run upstream unless shared. Operators like map and filter are suspending and backpressure-aware via suspension. StateFlow and SharedFlow provide hot replayable streams for UI state. terminal operators like collect or first consume the stream.

cards.question: Compare async/await pattern with coroutine async builder.
cards.answer: async starts deferred computation returning Deferred<T>; await retrieves result. Structured concurrency ties Deferred lifecycle to parent job. Use async for parallel independent calls then awaitAll. Avoid async without a scope on GlobalScope; it leaks work beyond UI or request lifetime.

cards.question: What is channel and when prefer it over Flow?
cards.answer: Channel is hot communication between producers and consumers with buffering strategies. Useful for event buses and worker queues bridging non-coroutine APIs. Flow models sequential data pipelines with clearer operator chains. Prefer Flow for transformations; Channel for fan-in fan-out between actors.

cards.question: How handle exceptions in coroutines with CoroutineExceptionHandler?
cards.answer: Uncaught exceptions in launch propagate to handler on root scope; async stores them until await. SupervisorJob plus handler logs errors without crashing unrelated tasks. try/catch around suspend calls handles expected failures. Never swallow CancellationException accidentally in generic catch blocks.

cards.question: What does suspendCoroutine do for callback APIs?
cards.answer: It bridges callback-based libraries into suspend functions by resuming continuation once. Used internally in retrofit and custom SDK wrappers. Must resume exactly once or the coroutine hangs or crashes. suspendCancellableCoroutine adds cancellation hooks when callbacks support abort.

cards.question: Why avoid GlobalScope in application code?
cards.answer: GlobalScope jobs live for process lifetime without structured parent cancellation. Leaks work after Activity or request ends, causing crashes or wasted battery. Inject application-scoped SupervisorJob tied to lifecycle instead. Tests become flaky when background GlobalScope tasks outlive test finish.

cards.question: How do you apply suspend functions in day-to-day Coroutines & Flow work?
cards.answer: suspend functions compile to state machines that pause at suspension points without blocking a thread. They must run inside a coroutine context and cooperate with cancellation at suspension boundaries. Bridge legacy callbacks with suspendCancellableCoroutine and resume exactly once.

cards.question: How does ViewModel survive configuration changes?
cards.answer: ViewModelStore retains instances across Activity recreation while process lives. ViewModel holds UI state and coroutine scopes cancelled on clear(). Do not hold Activity context references to avoid leaks. Hilt or manual factories inject repositories into ViewModels.

cards.question: What is StateFlow versus LiveData for UI state?
cards.answer: StateFlow is Kotlin coroutine-native hot flow with always-current value and conflation options. LiveData is lifecycle-aware and main-thread focused with simpler Java interop. StateFlow fits MVI and Compose; LiveData remains in legacy XML projects. Both should expose immutable state snapshots to UI.

cards.question: Explain Jetpack Compose recomposition basics.
cards.answer: Composable functions rerun when state they read changes, updating UI tree incrementally. remember stores mutable state across recompositions; derivedStateOf optimizes computed values. Side effects belong in LaunchedEffect or DisposableEffect with keys. Stable types help compiler skip unnecessary recomposition.

cards.question: How do you prevent memory leaks with coroutines on Android?
cards.answer: Bind coroutines to lifecycleScope or viewModelScope so they cancel when UI destroys. Avoid long-running GlobalScope launching from Fragments. Use weak references only as last resort; prefer architecture boundaries. LeakCanary detects retained contexts from static callbacks.

cards.question: What is Room and how does it use Kotlin?
cards.answer: Room generates SQLite access from interfaces with suspend queries and Flow return types. DAO methods map to compile-time verified SQL. Relations use data classes for nested projections. Migrations must be tested; destructive fallback is dev-only.

cards.question: How handle process death and saved state?
cards.answer: Persist critical UI state in SavedStateHandle or onSaveInstanceState bundles. Restore before rendering to avoid duplicate navigation events. Parcelable implementations via @Parcelize reduce boilerplate. Large data belongs in repository disk cache, not bundles.

cards.question: What patterns isolate domain logic from Android framework?
cards.answer: Pure Kotlin modules without Android dependencies hold use cases and entities. Data layer implements repositories with Retrofit, Room, and DataStore. Presentation maps domain models to UI state. Enables unit tests on JVM without Robolectric for business rules.

cards.question: How do WorkManager and coroutines interact?
cards.answer: CoroutineWorker implements doWork as suspend for async jobs with retries and constraints. Replaces deprecated AsyncTask patterns for deferrable background work. Constraints express network and battery requirements OS enforces. Idempotent work handles duplicate scheduling after crashes.

cards.question: What is dependency injection with Hilt at a high level?
cards.answer: Hilt generates Dagger components bound to Android classes like Application and Activity. @Inject constructors wire graphs at compile time with fail-fast missing bindings. Scopes align object lifetimes to components. Testing swaps modules with test installs for fakes.

cards.question: How optimize APK size when using Kotlin reflection-heavy libraries?
cards.answer: Enable R8 shrinking and keep rules for serialized models and DI generated classes. Avoid shipping unused kotlinx serialization or Ktor features via proguard consumer rules. App Bundle splits deliver language and density slices. Audit dependency tree for duplicate JSON parsers.

cards.question: How does Ktor structure an HTTP application?
cards.answer: Modules install features like ContentNegotiation, Authentication, and Routing. Routes define verbs and paths with suspend handlers. ApplicationEngine embeds Netty or CIO for async IO. Configuration loads from environment for twelve-factor deployment.

cards.question: What advantages does Spring Boot with Kotlin offer?
cards.answer: Null-safe domain models reduce defensive checks in services. Data classes map cleanly to DTOs with Jackson Kotlin module. Coroutines integrate via suspend controllers in Spring MVC 6+. Extension functions simplify configuration DSLs while keeping Java interop for libraries.

cards.question: How validate request bodies in Ktor or Spring?
cards.answer: Ktor uses receive<Type>() with kotlinx.serialization or Jackson and returns 400 on failure. Spring uses @Valid with Jakarta validation annotations on DTOs. Centralize error mapping to problem+json responses. Never trust client validation alone for security rules.

cards.question: Explain transaction boundaries with Spring @Transactional and coroutines.
cards.answer: Transactional proxies bind to thread-local sessions on blocking calls. Suspend functions need spring-data coroutine support or run blocking repos on IO dispatcher. Opening transactions across await points risks connection pool exhaustion. Keep transactions short around repository calls only.

cards.question: How serialize JSON with kotlinx.serialization versus Jackson?
cards.answer: kotlinx.serialization is compile-time plugin generating serializers with multiplatform support. Jackson is runtime reflection with mature ecosystem on JVM Spring apps. Choose kotlinx for KMP shared models; Jackson when integrating legacy Spring stacks. Explicit @Serializable handles versioning and unknown keys policy.

cards.question: What is Exposed ORM role in Kotlin backends?
cards.answer: Exposed offers type-safe DSL and DAO APIs over JDBC in pure Kotlin. Transactions wrap blocks with rollback on exceptions. Works well in Ktor services without JPA magic. For complex graphs JPA/Hibernate may still be chosen in Spring shops.

cards.question: How implement authentication in Ktor?

cards.question: What metrics and tracing hooks suit Kotlin microservices?
cards.answer: Micrometer integrates with Spring Boot Actuator exposing Prometheus metrics. OpenTelemetry Java agent traces Ktor and Spring HTTP with minimal code. Structured logging with MDC carries trace ids across coroutine context elements. Monitor connection pool saturation and GC pauses on JVM.

cards.question: How configure connection pools for database access?
cards.answer: HikariCP sizes pools from expected concurrency and DB limits, not thread count alone. Coroutines increase logical concurrency; pool must bound simultaneous connections. Timeouts prevent hung queries from starving pool. Health checks validate connectivity on startup and periodically.

cards.question: What is platform type when calling Java from Kotlin?
cards.answer: Java declarations without nullability annotations become flexible platform types. Kotlin compiler allows assignment to nullable or non-null Kotlin types at your risk. Add @Nullable/@NotNull in Java or wrap APIs with Kotlin extensions. NPE can still occur at Java boundaries if mismatched.

cards.question: How do @JvmStatic and @JvmOverloads help Java callers?
cards.answer: @JvmStatic exposes companion methods as static on the Java side. @JvmOverloads generates overloads for default parameter values Java lacks. @JvmName avoids signature clashes from erased generics. Essential for SDKs consumed by mixed Java/Kotlin codebases.

cards.question: When use fun interface SAM conversions?
cards.answer: Kotlin lambdas convert to Java functional interfaces automatically when marked fun interface. Simplifies Android listeners and executor callbacks. For multiple abstract methods Java interfaces need explicit object expressions. Kotlin 1.4+ fun interface reduces boilerplate for single-method APIs.

cards.question: What is Kotlin Multiplatform commonMain purpose?
cards.answer: Shared business logic compiles to JVM, JS, and native targets from one source set. expect/actual declarations abstract platform-specific APIs. Reduces duplicate models between Android and iOS when teams invest in KMP. Not all libraries are multiplatform-ready; check dependency support.

cards.question: How Gradle Kotlin DSL improves build scripts?
cards.answer: build.gradle.kts offers type-safe accessors and IDE completion versus Groovy DSL. Version catalogs centralize dependency coordinates in libs.versions.toml. Shared convention plugins enforce module standards. Same Gradle engine runs both DSL styles during migration.

cards.question: Explain JVM default method conflicts with Kotlin inheritance.
cards.answer: Java 8 interface defaults can clash when Kotlin classes implement multiple interfaces. Explicit override required in Kotlin to resolve diamond cases. @JvmDefaultWithoutCompatibility modes affect bytecode generation for older Android desugaring. Audit API surfaces when mixing Java 8 libraries.

cards.question: What causes Kotlin reflection performance cost?
cards.answer: KClass and callable references traverse metadata and box values. Prefer codegen with KSP or inline reified at hot paths. Serialization frameworks cache reflectively gathered adapters on first use. Benchmark startup impact on Android cold start when using heavy reflection.

cards.question: How tune JVM heap for Kotlin Spring services?
cards.answer: Set initial and max heap based on container limits leaving headroom for metaspace and native threads. G1GC is default on modern JDK; monitor pause times with GC logs. Avoid massive object graphs in session caches. Use virtual threads on JDK 21 for blocking IO heavy workloads.

cards.question: What is detekt and ktlint in Kotlin projects?
cards.answer: Static analysis enforces complexity limits, naming, and coroutine pitfalls. ktlint formats code to official style like prettier for Kotlin. Run in CI to block drift. Baseline files grandfather legacy issues during adoption.

cards.question: How publish a Kotlin library for Java consumers?
cards.answer: Ship JVM jar with Dokka-generated docs and explicit API files if using library authors plugin. Keep public API Java-friendly with annotations and avoid internal inline-only utilities leaking. Semantic versioning applies to ABI when exposing inline or inline value classes changes mangling.
